source.title: Leak@$k$: Unlearning Does Not Make LLMs Forget Under Probabilistic Decoding
source.authors: Hadi Reisizadeh; Jia-Jun Ruan; Yi-Wei Chen; Soumyadeep Pal; Si-Jia Liu; Ming-Yi Hong

page_placements.theme: Recovery by sampling or alternative decoding

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether unlearned models still reveal targeted knowledge under a different attack setting—repeated probabilistic sampling—rather than testing the listed fine-tuning, activation-editing, quantization, or prompting attacks.
record.gate_note: The measured attack is probabilistic decoding with repeated generations. It is not prompting-only, rephrasing, fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization; those specific attacks are not tested. The paper also reports many heatmaps whose exact cell values are not stated in the prose; these are not transcribed as numerical rows. The rows below retain endpoint values from Tables 5 and 6 and selected explicit WMDP results.
record.test_reason: The study re-evaluates unlearned checkpoints (NPO, BLUR-NPO, RMU and others) on TOFU, MUSE-News and WMDP under repeated probabilistic sampling (leak@k). This is a simple, different attack aimed at whether 'forgotten' knowledge is truly removed, so it bears on A. It also proposes RULE, which bears on F, but only against sampling. Sampling is a decoding-time attack, not rephrasing, jailbreaks, languages or in-context information, so it is not E. In the row fixes below, states for A rows describe whether A's effect (robust forgetting) holds, not whether leakage appears; this reverses the record's convention.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that methods that look successful under greedy decoding keep leaking under probabilistic sampling, rising with k, with top-p the main driver. RULE gives near-zero leakage on TOFU and the lowest leakage growth on MUSE-News. They treat WMDP NPO's zero leakage as over-forgetting. They do not adjust leakage for the Retrain reference, which itself reaches 0.622 on TOFU at k=128.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates existing unlearning checkpoints under probabilistic decoding and introduces RULE, a dynamic data-augmentation unlearning procedure; it does not reproduce the listed fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, or prompt attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Leakage depends on sampling budget k and decoding temperature T and top-p p; the paper says top-p is often the stronger driver. WMDP NPO differs from RMU, and RULE results differ by benchmark.

fits_no_version.finding: Repeated probabilistic decoding surfaces target answers that greedy decoding hides. Once a first sensitive token is sampled, later tokens become highly probable. Top-p drives leakage more than temperature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recovery by sampling: repeated stochastic decoding of an unlearned model restores forgotten answers beyond a retrain reference.

record.problems: Several benchmark results are presented in heatmaps without numerical values stated in the text; the selected table rows do not provide uncertainty estimates. Leakage scores depend on core evaluation metrics and judge models. WMDP NPO's no-leakage result is confounded by over-forgetting and gibberish output, as the authors state.
record.rows_left_out: The full endpoint-by-endpoint values for all methods and intermediate k values in Tables 5 and 6 were omitted to stay within the row limit; selected methods and k=1 and k=128 endpoints were retained. Additional temperature/top-p heatmap cells and the figures for TOFU and MUSE were not transcribed because exact values are not stated in the prose. MUSE retrain endpoint values were omitted because the flattened table layout does not permit reliable assignment.

untested.parts: MMLU/general utility numbers for the WMDP models are not reported. The listed fine-tuning, internal-edit, quantization and prompting attacks are not run.
No activation ablation or internal analysis.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attack; only decoding randomness.
RULE is tested only against repeated sampling, not against relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting, and only on TOFU and MUSE, not WMDP.

missing.what: TOFU Original row and other methods at k=1/128 (Original 0.288/0.886, GradDiff 0.261/0.835, NPO+ENT 0.246/0.764, LoUK 0.049/0.602, PMC 0.010/0.149) plus γ and retain columns
MUSE-News Retrain leak@k–RS values, needed as the reference for all MUSE rows
Average ES under greedy vs sampling barely changes (e.g. NPO 19.0% vs 20.5%, Retrain 8.3% vs 16.8%)
Refusal-option test: NPO picks E 94.2%, RMU 62.5%, Original 12.4%
RULE with NPO, SimNPO and RMU forget losses on TOFU (leak@128 vs retain)

record.verdict_notes: Key caveat: the Retrain model leaks heavily under sampling (TOFU 0.622 at k=128; MUSE Retrain examples also emit answers). Raw leak@k therefore overstates recovery, and the record's 'observed leakage' states ignored this. leak@k–Acc on 4-way multiple choice rises toward 1 for a chance-level sampler, so the RMU Acc curve is uninformative. Table A6 is labelled RULE-GradDiff, but its means (0.261…0.830) match GradDiff in Table 5, an internal inconsistency. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that targeted-knowledge accuracy is near chance while general ability is preserved as a joint prerequisite; tests leakage under repeated probabilistic decoding rather than the listed attack types.
No relearning fine-tuning attack on the unlearned model.
No activation-direction ablation or internal-edit experiment.
No recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Tests RULE against probabilistic multi-sampling leakage, not against the fine-tuning, internal-editing, quantization, or prompting attacks named in the claim.

rows.subject: Retrain
rows.note: Retrain excludes the forget set and is the paper's reference model.
rows.check: Retrain reference (leak@1–ES 0.169), not a test row. It is the baseline for TOFU rows r3–r8.

rows.subject: Retrain
rows.note: Reference score for a model retrained without the forget set.
rows.check: Retrain reference at k=128 (0.622). Even a model never trained on the forget set reaches 0.622, so raw leak@k overstates recovery. Original is 0.886.

rows.subject: NPO
rows.note: Leakage measure at one sampled generation.
rows.check: NPO k=1 is 0.206 vs Retrain 0.169 and Original 0.288. A single sample is close to Retrain. The record's 'partial' used leakage-as-effect; restated for A.

rows.subject: NPO
rows.note: The paper says existing methods increasingly leak as the number of generations increases.
rows.check: NPO k=128 is 0.745 vs Retrain 0.622 and Original 0.886. Excess over Retrain is about 0.12, roughly half the Original–Retrain gap. That is partial recovery, not full; the record said 'observed' leakage with no baseline.

rows.subject: BLUR-NPO
rows.note: Leakage is lower than for several other unlearning methods at this setting.
rows.check: BLUR-NPO k=1 is 0.109, below Retrain 0.169. No leakage beyond the reference.

rows.subject: BLUR-NPO
rows.note: Leakage increases substantially across the reported sampling budget.
rows.check: BLUR-NPO k=128 is 0.552, below Retrain 0.622. The sampling attack shows no recovery beyond the reference on this measure. The record's 'partial' ignored the Retrain baseline.

rows.subject: RULE-GradDiff
rows.note: The paper describes RULE-GradDiff as achieving almost zero leakage.
rows.check: RULE-GradDiff (the study's own method) k=1 is 0.001 vs Retrain 0.169. Robust only to sampling. It may undershoot Retrain, i.e. over-forget, though retain ES is 0.397, the highest in Table 5.

rows.subject: RULE-GradDiff
rows.note: The paper reports almost zero leakage for RULE-GradDiff even at 128 generations; the table value is 0.041.
rows.check: RULE-GradDiff k=128 is 0.041, far below Retrain 0.622. Resistance to the sampling attack is essentially full, so 'partial' is wrong. It is the study's own method; F is tested only against sampling.

rows.subject: RULE-NPO
rows.note: RULE-NPO reduces leakage relative to several methods but leakage remains and rises with k.
rows.check: RULE-NPO k=128 is 0.68, below BLUR-NPO 0.79 and Original 0.97 but far from zero. There is no Retrain baseline, so read as partial robustness relative to the other methods.

rows.subject: RMU
rows.operation_detail: leak@k–Acc on WMDP-bio under probabilistic decoding
rows.baseline: greedy decoding score for NPO: 26% (not RMU)
rows.note: The text says RMU shows a leakage trend as k increases; top-p has stronger influence than temperature.
rows.check: The baseline is wrong: 26% is NPO's score, and chance is 25%. Under sampling, leak@k–Acc rises toward 1 even for a chance-level model, since the max over k draws of a 4-way guess approaches 1. A rising curve doesn't show recovered knowledge, and the value is figure-only.

rows.subject: RMU
rows.operation_detail: LLM-judge leakage under free-form probabilistic generation
rows.note: The text describes nearly no leakage at (T, p) = (0.2, 0.2) and a clear leakage trend at (1.0, 1.0).
rows.check: RMU free-form LJ: minimal leakage at (0.2,0.2), a clear rise at (1.0,1.0). Figure only, with no base-model or retrain reference. A holds under low randomness only.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 7 caption and WMDP free-form paragraph (Section 3)

rows.subject: NPO
rows.operation_detail: leak@k–Acc on WMDP-bio under probabilistic decoding
rows.value: flat across all k and (T, p) pairs
rows.note: The authors attribute the flat result to over-forgetting disrupting answer selection.
rows.check: NPO WMDP Acc is flat at 26% (≈chance) across all k and (T,p), so forgetting is robust to sampling. But the authors attribute this to over-forgetting: NPO picks the refusal option E 94.2% of the time (Table A9). General ability is not shown to be kept.

source_check.locator_found: WMDP paragraph: flat across all k and (T,p), matching greedy 26%

rows.subject: NPO
rows.operation_detail: LLM-judge leakage under free-form probabilistic generation
rows.note: NPO generates gibberish responses; the authors describe this as over-forgetting and report no observable leakage by LJ.
rows.check: NPO LJ is 0 because outputs are gibberish or masked (Table A10). No leakage, but general generation quality is degraded, contrary to A's 'keeps general ability'.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on versions A and F.

tranche.reason: It re-evaluates unlearned checkpoints with a different attack (repeated probabilistic sampling, leak@k) aimed at the same question. It also proposes RULE.

source_check.notes: TOFU Retrain itself rises 0.169 to 0.622 under T=p=1.0, so read leakage against it. Table A6 (25-seed std, labelled RULE-GradDiff) has means 0.261-0.830, matching plain GradDiff in Table 5, not RULE-GradDiff (0.001-0.041), so it is probably mislabelled and RULE's uncertainty is thin. MUSE Retrain is only in the Fig. 5 heatmaps (no values in text). Authors say BLUR-NPO begins to fail at (0.8,1.0) (Table 4 example). RULE is the authors' own method.

statements.correction: TOFU NPO (LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct, T=p=1.0) leak@k-ES 0.206 at k=1, 0.745 at k=128; Retrain 0.169 and 0.622; Original 0.288 and 0.886. Excess over Retrain about 0.12, roughly half the Original-Retrain gap (0.264).
statements.problem: Numbers right, but it sits under a 'challenges' label. NPO is near Retrain at k=1 (0.206 vs 0.169), and at k=128 it is 0.745 vs Retrain 0.622: partial recovery (limits_scope), not effect absent.

statements.correction: Add the claim, don't drop it. RULE-GradDiff, TOFU, LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct: leak@128-ES 0.041. RULE-NPO, MUSE-News, LLaMA2-7B: leak@k-RS 0.15 at k=1, 0.68 at k=128 (BLUR-NPO 0.79, Original 0.97), T=p=1.0. Loss, model and core metric differ. No Retrain value in Table 6.
statements.problem: It cites r15,r16 (RULE-NPO) but says nothing about this study. The rows do fit the bullet's theme: RULE's near-zero leakage on TOFU does not carry over to MUSE-News.
